label: Random walk with and without drift — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: For the random walk yₜ = μ + yₜ₋₁ + εₜ with E(εₜ) = 0 and E(εₜ²) = σ²ₑ, the mean and variance of yₜ are:
items.explanation: Unrolling gives yₜ = tμ + Σεᵢ, so the mean is tμ and, since the shocks are uncorrelated, the variance is tσ²ₑ. Both grow with t, which is the signature of a random walk. This is June 2026 Q23; the options with one moment held constant are the traps.

items.stem: For the random walk yₜ = yₜ₋₁ + εₜ with no drift, E(yₜ) and Var(yₜ) are:
items.explanation: The shocks have mean zero so the mean stays at 0, but their variances still accumulate to tσ². A constant mean with a growing variance is still non-stationary — only one of the three conditions has to fail. Simulated at t = 20 with σ = 2: mean −0.0102 and variance 79.89 against 0 and 80.

items.stem: Weak stationarity requires the autocovariance to depend on:
items.explanation: Together with a constant mean and a constant finite variance, that is the definition. The random walk's Corr(yₜ, yₜ₊ₖ) = √(t/(t+k)) depends on t as well as the lag, which is precisely why it fails.

items.stem: A random walk becomes stationary after:
items.explanation: Δyₜ = yₜ − yₜ₋₁ = μ + εₜ, which is white noise plus a constant and therefore stationary. Differencing twice would over-difference, introducing a non-invertible moving-average component.

items.stem: In a random walk, the effect of a single shock on future values is:
items.explanation: The coefficient on yₜ₋₁ is exactly 1, so a shock is carried forward undiminished: its impact k periods later is 1ᵏ = 1. Geometric decay at rate φᵏ is what happens in a STATIONARY AR(1) with |φ| < 1, which is the contrast worth holding.

items.stem: ARIMA(0, 1, 0) describes:
items.explanation: No AR terms, one difference, no MA terms. Differencing once leaves Δyₜ = εₜ, which is white noise, so the series is integrated of order 1 with nothing else in the model.

items.stem: For a random walk, Corr(yₜ, yₜ₊ₖ) equals:
items.explanation: Cov(yₜ, yₜ₊ₖ) = tσ², since the two sums share their first t shocks, and dividing by √(tσ² · (t+k)σ²) gives √(t/(t+k)). Option B is the stationary AR(1)'s autocorrelation. Simulated: t = 10, k = 5 gave 0.8164 against 0.8165; t = 20, k = 20 gave 0.7070 against 0.7071.

items.stem: For a driftless random walk, Corr(y₂₅, y₁₀₀) equals:
items.explanation: √(t/(t+k)) with t = 25 and t + k = 100 gives √(25/100) = √0.25 = 0.5 exactly. Option A is the ratio t/(t+k) without the square root, which is the standard slip.
items.check: The correlation must exceed the variance ratio 0.25, since taking a square root of a number below 1 increases it.

items.stem: The series yₜ = 5 + 0.2t + εₜ is:
items.explanation: Its mean 5 + 0.2t is not constant, so it is not stationary; but its variance is σ² throughout and its autocovariance depends only on the lag, so subtracting the deterministic line leaves a stationary series. The correct repair is to de-trend, not to difference — differencing would over-difference.

items.stem: Over-differencing a stationary series produces:
options: a unit root in the AR part
items.explanation: Differencing white noise gives Δyₜ = εₜ − εₜ₋₁, an MA(1) with θ = 1 — exactly on the invertibility boundary |θ| < 1. The variance doubles to 2σ² and a lag-1 autocorrelation of −0.5 appears. Simulated: variance 2.0102 against 2, and ρ₁ = −0.4998 against −0.5.

items.stem: For a Gaussian process, weak stationarity implies:
items.explanation: A Gaussian process is completely determined by its mean function and its autocovariance function, so if both are shift-invariant then every joint distribution is too. For a non-Gaussian process weak stationarity implies nothing further — the skewness, for instance, could still change with t.

items.stem: Consider the driftless random walk yₜ = yₜ₋₁ + εₜ.
items.explanation: A is true — the mean condition holds. B is true, and it is the reason stationarity fails. C is true: the covariance depends on t. D is false — one differencing suffices, since Δyₜ = εₜ is already white noise.
statements: Var(yₜ) = tσ², so the variance is not constant.
Cov(yₜ, yₜ₊ₖ) = tσ², which depends on t and not only on the lag.
Two differencings are needed to make it stationary.

A.why: True. The shocks have mean zero, so the first condition for weak stationarity actually holds — which is why a constant mean alone proves nothing.

B.why: True. Variances of uncorrelated shocks accumulate, giving tσ², and that failure alone destroys stationarity.

C.why: True. The two sums share their first t shocks, so the covariance is tσ² — a function of the earlier time point rather than of the separation.

D.why: False. One differencing gives Δyₜ = εₜ, which is white noise. A second differencing would over-difference and introduce a non-invertible MA component.

items.stem: For a random walk with μ = 0.3 and σ² = 4, the mean and variance of y₁₀ are:
items.explanation: E(y₁₀) = tμ = 10 × 0.3 = 3 and Var(y₁₀) = tσ² = 10 × 4 = 40. Both are t times the one-step quantity, so the standard deviation at t = 10 is √40 ≈ 6.32.
items.check: Both moments must be exactly ten times their one-step values, which rules out any option holding one of them fixed.

items.stem: For a driftless random walk at t = 100, the autocorrelations at lags 1 and 20 are approximately:
items.explanation: √(100/101) = 0.9950 and √(100/120) = 0.9129. Option B is a stationary AR(1) with φ = 0.9, whose lag-20 autocorrelation is 0.9²⁰ = 0.122 — the contrast that makes a slowly decaying sample ACF the practical signal of a unit root.
items.check: At lag 50 the value would be √(100/150) = 0.816, still high — the decay is extremely slow by design.

items.stem: Which pair of series has the same mean path but requires opposite repairs?
options: yₜ = 5 + 0.2t + εₜ and yₜ = 0.2 + yₜ₋₁ + εₜ
yₜ = yₜ₋₁ + εₜ and yₜ = 2yₜ₋₁ + εₜ
items.explanation: Both have a mean rising at 0.2 per period, but the first is trend-stationary with constant variance σ² and reverts to its line, while the second is a random walk with drift, variance tσ², which never reverts. De-trend the first and difference the second; each wrong choice leaves its own characteristic damage.

items.stem: A stationary AR(1) with φ = 0.99 has variance σ²/(1 − φ²). How does it compare with a random walk's?
options: about 100σ², finite, against the random walk's σ²
about 50σ², finite, against the random walk's unbounded tσ²
smaller than the random walk's at every t
items.explanation: 1/(1 − 0.99²) = 1/0.0199 = 50.25, so the variance is about 50σ² — large but finite, and the process does eventually revert. At φ = 1 the formula breaks down and the variance is tσ², growing without bound. The qualitative change happens at a single point.
items.check: A random walk's variance exceeds 50σ² once t > 50, so option D fails for large t and holds only early on.

items.stem: Consider regressing one random walk on an independent other.
items.explanation: A is true — the rejection rate tends to 1. B is true: the residuals are non-stationary so the standard error is the thing that fails. C is true, and it is what cointegration tests for. D is false — differencing both is valid for inference but answers a question about changes, discarding any long-run relationship.
statements: The proportion of samples in which the slope appears significant tends to 1 as n grows.
What fails is the standard error, because the regression residuals are themselves non-stationary.
If some linear combination of the two series is stationary, a levels relationship is real.
Differencing both series is always the best repair.

A.why: True. The t-statistic diverges like √n rather than converging to a fixed distribution, so more data makes the spurious relationship look stronger, not weaker.

B.why: True. The usual formula assumes stationary errors of finite variance; with non-stationary residuals the quantity divided by n never settles, so the yardstick is wrong by a factor that grows.

C.why: True — that is the definition of cointegration. The two series wander, but they wander together and the gap between them reverts, so a relationship between levels genuinely exists.

D.why: False. Differencing is always valid for inference, but it answers a question about short-run changes and discards any long-run levels relationship. Where cointegration is present, that relationship is exactly what is of interest.

items.stem: Differencing a white-noise series yₜ = εₜ gives a series whose variance and lag-1 autocorrelation are:
items.explanation: Δyₜ = εₜ − εₜ₋₁ has variance σ² + σ² = 2σ², and Cov(Δyₜ, Δyₜ₋₁) = −σ², giving an autocorrelation of −σ²/2σ² = −0.5. So differencing has doubled the variance and manufactured a correlation. Simulated: 2.0102 and −0.4998.
items.check: This is an MA(1) with θ = 1, whose theoretical ρ₁ is −θ/(1+θ²) = −1/2 ✓ — and θ = 1 is exactly on the invertibility boundary.

items.stem: The variance of a k-step-ahead forecast error from a random walk is:
items.explanation: The k-step error is the sum of the next k shocks, so its variance is kσ² and the interval widens like √k forever. For a stationary process the forecast error variance rises to a ceiling, namely the process variance σ²/(1 − φ²). That contrast is the practical cost of a unit root: long-horizon forecasts from a random walk carry no useful precision.

items.stem: A forecaster differences every series by default. One model then shows residual lag-1 autocorrelation near −0.5 and an estimated MA coefficient near 1. The best reading is:
options: the model needs an extra AR term
the series was already stationary and has been over-differenced
the shocks are not white noise
items.explanation: Those two figures are the fingerprint of over-differencing: differencing a stationary series doubles its variance and produces an MA(1) with θ = 1 and ρ₁ = −0.5. The remedy is to undo the differencing, not to add terms. Note the contrast with under-differencing, which leaves a slowly decaying ACF and a near-unit AR root — so the two errors are distinguishable.
